runs.t: Mary put the letter down in the yard and waited. Jack had never wanted any of this, and yet Jack now stood under the bridge. Emma searched for the sack of salt for a long time behind the wall, without success.

Someone had closed the shutters without giving a reason. The fire crackled in the stove, and the shadows wandered across the wall. Emma arrived at the well when Robert had already left. Jack searched for the rope for a long time by the lighthouse, without success. “It has grown late,” said Robert, and looked at Alice. Robert arrived up on the pass when Tom had already left.

The next day Alice set off with the key under one arm, without saying goodbye. Outside the rain fell against the shutters, steady and unhurried. The wind turned, and with it the mood in the house. “It has grown late,” said Emma. “I do not know,” Tom replied. Emma had never wanted any of this, and yet Emma now stood under the bridge. Far below in the valley a bell struck, then again, then no more.

The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. Mary had never wanted any of this, and yet Mary now stood at the well. The fire crackled in the stove, and the shadows wandered across the wall. “Wait until tomorrow,” said Tom, and looked at Robert. For a while nobody said anything, and that was worse than any word.

Emma searched for the coat for a long time under the bridge, without success. The way was longer than it had looked on the map. The next day Emma set off with the map under one arm, without saying goodbye.

For a while nobody said anything, and that was worse than any word. Mary had never wanted any of this, and yet Mary now stood in the stable. Mary put the barrel down at the well and waited. Robert had never wanted any of this, and yet Robert now stood at the well. Snow lay on the yard in the morning, and nobody had heard it come.

On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch. It was a grey noon, and under the bridge nothing stirred. Jack had never wanted any of this, and yet Jack now stood at the well. Alice arrived by the lighthouse when Robert had already left. The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. In Saltmere, it was said, Alice had last seen the barrel.

The water stood high that year, higher than anyone could remember. Emma had never wanted any of this, and yet Emma now stood under the bridge. Tom arrived behind the wall when Mary had already left. Whoever found the letter, said Jack, was to tell Tom. Snow lay on the yard in the morning, and nobody had heard it come.

The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. Jack did not answer. Alice asked again, more quietly this time. It was a clear evening, and by the lighthouse nothing stirred. The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. “You should have come sooner,” said Jack. “Nobody asked us,” Alice replied. On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch.

For a while nobody said anything, and that was worse than any word. Robert did not answer. Tom asked again, more quietly this time. It smelled of wet wood, of salt and of old paper. At the harbour, it was said, Jack had last seen the key.
